questions.question: What are the main database replication strategies and when do you use each?
questions.title: Database Replication: Master-Slave, Master-Master, and Quorum Reads
questions.direct_answer: Three main strategies: **single-leader (master-slave)** — one writer, many read replicas, simple and consistent on writes but read-after-write lag; **multi-leader (master-master)** — writers in multiple regions, low-latency global writes but conflicts to reconcile; **leaderless / quorum (Dynamo-style)** — any node accepts writes, consistency tuned via R+W>N. Pick **single-leader** for most relational workloads (Postgres/MySQL with read replicas), **multi-leader** for active-active multi-region with low-conflict workloads, and **leaderless** for high-availability key-value stores (DynamoDB, Cassandra) that need to survive entire-region failures.

interviewer_intent.testing: Understanding of three replication topologies, their consistency/latency/availability trade-offs, and conflict resolution.
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Conflating sync vs async replication with the topology choice, or assuming master-master means strong consistency across regions.
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Walk through quorum math (R+W>N for strong reads), discuss conflict resolution strategies (LWW, vector clocks, CRDTs), and explain semi-sync replication as a middle ground for the leader-failure data-loss problem.

sections.title: Why Replicate at All
sections.content:
Replication serves three goals — you usually want all three but they pull in different directions:

- **Durability:** survive disk/server/AZ/region loss without data loss.
- **Availability:** keep serving reads (and ideally writes) when any one replica fails.
- **Read scalability:** spread read load across many replicas.

The choice of replication topology determines:
- Whether writes are accepted in one place or many.
- How fresh the replicas are (sync vs async).
- What happens during a partition (CP vs AP from CAP).
- How conflicts are reconciled (or avoided).

sections.title: Single-Leader (Master-Slave) Replication
sections.content:
**Topology:** ```mermaid flowchart LR Client([Clients]) Leader[(Leader
writes + reads)] F1[(Follower 1
reads)] F2[(Follower 2
reads)] F3[(Follower 3
reads)] Client -->|writes| Leader Client -->|reads| F1 Client -->|reads| F2 Client -->|reads| F3 Leader -.async/sync replication.-> F1 Leader -.async/sync replication.-> F2 Leader -.async/sync replication.-> F3 classDef leader fill:#fee2e2,stroke:#ef4444 classDef follower fill:#dbeafe,stroke:#3b82f6 class Leader leader class F1,F2,F3 follower ``` - One node (the leader) accepts all writes; followers replicate from leader. - Reads can go to leader (strong) or followers (eventual). - Examples: PostgreSQL streaming replication, MySQL primary/replica, MongoDB replica set, Redis primary/replica. **Sync modes:** - **Async:** leader commits + acks client without waiting for followers. Fast writes, risk of data loss on leader crash. - **Sync:** leader waits for all followers (or quorum) before acking. Slow writes, durable. - **Semi-sync (PostgreSQL/MySQL):** leader waits for at least one follower; balances durability and latency. **Pros:** simple, consistent on writes, easy to reason about. **Cons:** writes don't scale beyond what one leader can handle; failover takes seconds-to-minutes; followers lag (read-after-write inconsistency).

sections.title: Read-After-Write Consistency — The Big Single-Leader Trap
sections.content:
**The problem:** user posts a tweet (write to leader), refreshes the page (read from a follower), doesn't see their own tweet because the follower hasn't replicated yet.

**Solutions, weakest to strongest:**

1. **Read-from-leader after write** — for some time window after a write (e.g., 30s), route the same user's reads to the leader. Defeats some read scaling.
2. **Sticky session to leader** — always serve a particular user from the leader. Coarse but simple.
3. **Wait-for-replica with version tokens** — client receives a write LSN; subsequent reads pass it; replica blocks until it has caught up.
4. **Synchronous replication** — follower commit before client ack. Strongest, slowest.

**Monotonic-reads consistency:** even on followers, route the same user to the same follower (sticky), so they don't see the data appear, then disappear (when one follower is more up-to-date than another).

sections.title: Multi-Leader (Master-Master) Replication
sections.content:
**Topology:** ```mermaid flowchart LR USClient([US Clients]) EUClient([EU Clients]) USLeader[(US Leader
writes + reads)] EULeader[(EU Leader
writes + reads)] USClient --> USLeader EUClient --> EULeader USLeader <-->|async bi-directional
replication| EULeader classDef leader fill:#fee2e2,stroke:#ef4444 class USLeader,EULeader leader ``` - Multiple leaders, typically one per region, all accepting writes. - Bi-directional async replication between leaders. - Examples: PostgreSQL with BDR, MySQL Galera Cluster, CouchDB, multi-master Cassandra, DynamoDB Global Tables. **Pros:** - Low write latency for users worldwide (write to nearest region). - Survives region failure with active capacity elsewhere. - Higher write throughput aggregate. **Cons:** - **Conflicts** — two regions write to the same row simultaneously; which wins? - Replication lag means a user in region B might briefly not see region A's write. - Operationally complex (which region won that conflict last week?). **Conflict resolution strategies:** - **Last-write-wins (LWW)** — keep the write with latest timestamp. Simple but loses data on concurrent writes. - **Application-level merge** — surface conflict to app code (CouchDB style). - **CRDTs** — mathematically guaranteed merge (counters, sets, sequences). - **Avoid by routing** — partition writes by user/key so the same key only ever writes to one leader.

sections.title: Leaderless (Quorum / Dynamo-Style) Replication
sections.content:
**Topology:** ```mermaid flowchart TB Client([Client]) Coord[Coordinator
any node] R1[(Replica 1)] R2[(Replica 2)] R3[(Replica 3)] Client --> Coord Coord -->|write to W replicas| R1 Coord -->|write to W replicas| R2 Coord -->|write to W replicas| R3 Coord -.read from R replicas.-> R1 Coord -.read from R replicas.-> R2 classDef coord fill:#fef3c7,stroke:#f59e0b classDef replica fill:#dbeafe,stroke:#3b82f6 class Coord coord class R1,R2,R3 replica ``` - No leader; client (or coordinator node) sends writes to **all N replicas** in parallel; commits when **W** replicas ack. - Reads sent to **all N replicas**; client merges responses from **R** replicas. - Examples: DynamoDB, Cassandra, Riak. **Quorum math: R + W > N** - N = total replicas (typically 3). - W = write replicas (typically 2). - R = read replicas (typically 2). - R + W > N → read and write sets overlap by at least one node → reads see latest write. **Tunable per operation:** - `R=W=1, N=3` → fast, eventual consistency. - `R=W=2, N=3` → strong consistency on each operation, still tolerant to one failure. - `R=W=3, N=3` → strict but no failure tolerance. - `R=1, W=3` → fast reads, durable writes (read-mostly workload). **Pros:** survives multiple failures, no failover needed, tunable consistency. **Cons:** consistency is per-operation, not global; conflicts still possible (concurrent writes); operationally complex.

sections.title: Conflict Resolution — Going Deeper
sections.content:
**Last-write-wins (LWW)**
- Each write tagged with a timestamp; conflict winner = highest timestamp.
- Simple. **Bad in distributed systems** because clocks drift; recent writes can be silently overwritten.
- Used by Cassandra default.

**Vector clocks**
- Each replica maintains a counter per replica; writes carry the vector.
- Two writes are **concurrent** if neither vector strictly dominates the other.
- Concurrent writes are surfaced to the application for resolution.
- Used by DynamoDB (early), Riak.

**Hybrid Logical Clocks (HLC)**
- Combines wall clock + logical counter; provides causality with bounded skew.
- Used by CockroachDB, MongoDB.

**CRDTs (Conflict-free Replicated Data Types)**
- Data structures designed to merge automatically without conflict.
- Counters (G-Counter, PN-Counter), sets (G-Set, OR-Set), sequences (Logoot, RGA).
- Used by Riak, Redis CRDTs (Enterprise), collaborative editors (Figma, Google Docs).

**Operational transformation (OT)**
- Transform operations to commute; older approach used by Google Docs (now moving to CRDTs).

sections.title: Sync vs Async — Orthogonal to Topology
sections.content:
**Async replication**
- Writer doesn't wait for replicas. Low latency.
- Risk: leader crashes after ack but before replication → data loss.
- Used by default in MySQL, PostgreSQL, MongoDB.

**Sync replication**
- Writer waits for ALL replicas. No data loss but a single slow replica blocks every write.
- Rarely used pure-form due to latency/availability cost.

**Semi-sync / quorum-sync**
- Writer waits for AT LEAST ONE (or quorum) of the replicas. Bounded data-loss risk; bounded latency.
- PostgreSQL `synchronous_commit=on` with `synchronous_standby_names`.
- MySQL semi-sync replication.
- Spanner / Raft / Paxos systems are inherently quorum-sync.

**Recommendation:** semi-sync (one replica must ack) for production relational DBs — balances durability and write latency.

sections.title: Failure Modes and Operational Realities
sections.content:
**Single-leader: leader failure**
- Detect via heartbeat timeout.
- Promote a follower (manual or automated via Patroni, Orchestrator, RDS managed failover).
- Risk: split-brain if the old leader comes back — STONITH (Shoot The Other Node In The Head) or fencing tokens.
- Recent writes may be lost if async replication.

**Multi-leader: conflict storms**
- During network partition, both regions accept writes; on heal, conflicts may be many.
- Strategy: route writes by partition key so same row only writes to one region; conflicts only happen at boundary cases.

**Leaderless: read repair and anti-entropy**
- Read repair: if reads return inconsistent values, write the latest back to lagging replicas.
- Anti-entropy: background process compares replicas and reconciles (Cassandra repair, Riak active anti-entropy).

**Cascading replication failure**
- Followers lag behind → leader's WAL grows → leader runs out of disk → outage.
- Monitor replication lag; alert before lag becomes critical.

sections.title: Key Points
sections.content:
- **Single-leader** — one writer, many readers; simple, default for relational; read-after-write lag is the main hazard.
- **Multi-leader** — multiple regional writers; low write latency globally; conflicts need resolution.
- **Leaderless / quorum** — any node writes; tune consistency via R+W>N; survives multi-node failure.
- **Sync vs async is orthogonal** to topology; semi-sync is the practical sweet spot for relational.
- **Conflict resolution:** LWW is simple but lossy; vector clocks expose concurrent writes; CRDTs auto-merge.
- **Read-after-write consistency** — stick session to leader, use version tokens, or accept eventual.
- **Match topology to use case:** relational + read-scale = single-leader; global active-active = multi-leader; max availability = leaderless.

sections.title: How to Answer This Verbally
sections.content:
**Three topologies**

**Single-leader (master-slave):**
- One leader takes all writes; followers replicate; reads can hit any node
- Examples: Postgres, MySQL, MongoDB, Redis
- Pros: simple, consistent writes, easy to reason about
- Cons: writes capped at one node; failover takes time; follower lag causes read-after-write issues

**Multi-leader (master-master):**
- Multiple leaders, typically one per region; bi-directional async replication
- Examples: Postgres BDR, MySQL Galera, CouchDB, DynamoDB Global Tables
- Pros: low write latency globally, survives region failure with hot capacity elsewhere
- Cons: conflicts on concurrent writes need resolution; operationally complex

**Leaderless (Dynamo-style quorum):**
- No leader; coordinator writes to N replicas in parallel, commits when W ack; reads from R replicas, merges
- Examples: DynamoDB, Cassandra, Riak
- Pros: survives multi-node failure, no failover needed, tunable consistency per operation
- Cons: consistency is per-op not global; concurrent-write conflicts still possible

**Quorum math — R + W > N**

With N=3 replicas, the standard is R=W=2. Read and write sets overlap by at least one node, so reads see the latest write. Tunable: R=1 W=3 for read-heavy, R=W=1 for fastest+eventual, R=W=3 for strict but no failure tolerance.

**The single-leader trap — read-after-write**

User posts tweet to leader, refreshes, hits a follower that hasn't replicated yet, doesn't see their own tweet. Solutions: read-from-leader for 30s after write; sticky session; pass write LSN as version token, replica waits until caught up; synchronous replication.

Monotonic reads: route the same user to the same follower, so they don't see data appear and then disappear.

**Multi-leader conflicts**

Resolution strategies:
- Last-write-wins (LWW): timestamp-based; bad because clock skew loses data
- Vector clocks: track causality; concurrent writes surfaced to app code
- HLC (Hybrid Logical Clocks): wall + logical, bounded skew
- CRDTs: data structures that merge mathematically (counters, sets, collaborative-editor sequences)
- Avoid: route writes by partition key so each row only writes to one leader

**Sync vs async — orthogonal to topology**

- Async: low latency, risk of data loss on leader crash. Default in most relational DBs.
- Sync (all replicas): no data loss but a slow replica blocks every write. Rarely pure-form.
- Semi-sync (one replica must ack): bounded data-loss + bounded latency. Production sweet spot.

Spanner and Raft systems are inherently quorum-sync.

**Failure modes**

Single-leader: failover via Patroni/Orchestrator; STONITH or fencing for split-brain prevention; recent writes lost if async.

Multi-leader: partition causes conflict storms on heal; mitigation = partition by key.

Leaderless: read repair (write latest back to lagging replicas during reads) + anti-entropy background reconciliation.

Cascade: follower lag → leader WAL grows → leader OOMs disk. Monitor lag and alert early.

**Match topology to use case**

- Relational with read-scale needs → single-leader Postgres/MySQL with replicas + semi-sync
- Global low-latency writes, low-conflict workload → multi-leader, partition by region
- Max availability + scale, key-value workload → leaderless Cassandra/DynamoDB with R+W>N

**Recommendation**

**Default to single-leader for transactional/relational workloads (Postgres or MySQL with one or two replicas, semi-sync replication, read-after-write via sticky session or LSN token). Reach for multi-leader only when global write latency requires it and you can route by key to avoid conflicts. Use leaderless quorum (Cassandra/DynamoDB) for high-availability key-value workloads where R+W>N gives you tunable consistency per operation. The replication topology determines your CAP/PACELC posture — pick deliberately.**
